title: Path traversal in static data loader
description: The exported loader accepts a caller-controlled `file` value and appends it directly to the static-data path. Because `path.resolve` normalizes `..` segments and there is no allowlist or traversal rejection, a caller can escape `./data/static/` and read other local files whose names can satisfy the appended `.yml` suffix. The file contents are then returned after YAML parsing, exposing unintended local data and allowing attacker-controlled files to influence application data if the caller relies on this loader for trusted static records.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the exported function's `file` parameter; no validation is performed at the function boundary.

The untrusted parameter is concatenated into a filesystem path before resolution. Values containing `../` can traverse above `./data/static/`; `path.resolve` normalizes rather than constrains the result.
The resolved attacker-influenced path is passed to `readFile`, which reads the unintended local `.yml` file and forwards its contents to YAML parsing.

title: Unrestricted request-body properties forwarded by address update service
description: Address mutations forward the caller's entire params object directly to the backend. Because there is no explicit client-side allow-list, callers of this exported service method can submit arbitrary address-model properties, including fields the UI may not intend to expose. If the corresponding API persists the body without its own property-level authorization, an attacker can set protected fields such as ownership, verification, or internal status fields. This file does not show the backend enforcement, so exploitability is dependent on the API implementation.

trace.description: The exported put(id, params) method receives params from a caller outside this file; the parameter is not restricted to an explicit set of address properties.
The caller-supplied params object is forwarded unchanged as the HTTP PUT body, with no property allow-list or filtering in the service.
HttpClient sends the unrestricted object to the Address API, where backend model binding may persist attacker-supplied protected properties if server-side property authorization is absent.

title: Caller-controlled basket identifiers are used without object ownership enforcement
description: Basket and basket-item identifiers arrive as parameters from callers outside this file and are inserted directly into requests. The service performs no ownership check tying the requested basket or item to the authenticated user. Consequently, if the corresponding API endpoints do not independently enforce object-level authorization, a user can substitute another user's basket or basket-item ID to read, modify, delete, apply a coupon to, or check out that resource. The same client-side trust assumption applies to the target basket used during guest-basket merging.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file supplies the basket or basket-item identifier to the exported service methods, including find(id), get(id), put(id, params), del(id), checkout(id), and applyCoupon(id, coupon).
The supplied identifier is propagated into the request path without any ownership, authenticated-user, or role check in the service.
The identifier reaches the GET basket endpoint, allowing the caller to request an arbitrary basket ID unless server-side authorization independently rejects it.

title: Guest-basket merge trusts an arbitrary target basket
description: mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket accepts targetBasketId from a caller outside this file, reads that basket, and then uses its returned item IDs to issue updates. For new items it also sends targetBasketId as the BasketId field. No invariant verifies that targetBasketId belongs to the current user before these operations. An attacker able to invoke this service with another user's basket ID can cause guest items to be merged into or mutate that basket if the backend relies on the client to select an authorized target.

trace.description: Entrypoint: a caller outside this file supplies targetBasketId to mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket.
The caller-supplied targetBasketId is used to fetch the target basket, and the resulting item IDs and quantities are then used to construct mutation requests without an ownership check.
For products not already present, the target basket ID is sent as BasketId in a create request; no authorization decision is made in this file.

title: Unbounded chat request and streaming response consumption
description: The exported streamMessages method accepts an arbitrary-length messages array and sends it directly as the request body to the chat endpoint. It does not enforce a maximum number of messages, content length, or token budget. During streaming, every parsed response chunk is appended to the in-memory chunks array and retained until yielded; there is likewise no response-size, chunk-count, timeout, or tool-call limit. A caller of this frontend service can submit very large prompts or induce a very large/long-running stream, increasing backend/LLM token consumption and client memory use. Server-side limits or infrastructure throttling may mitigate the issue, but they are not present or verifiable in this file.

trace.description: Caller outside this file invokes the exported streamMessages method with a caller-controlled messages array; the method imposes no size, count, or token limit.
The complete messages array is placed directly into the POST body for the chat/LLM endpoint without truncation, token accounting, or a request-size guard.

Each received streaming response is appended to the chunks array, and the loop retains chunks until they are yielded; there is no maximum response size, chunk count, or timeout limiting memory and processing consumption.

title: Unbounded synchronous conversation storage enables client-side resource exhaustion
description: The service synchronously serializes and persists an arbitrarily large caller-supplied conversation, together with all previously stored conversations, without enforcing a size or count limit. A caller outside this file that can invoke save can provide very large message/title/content fields or repeatedly add conversations. JSON.stringify and localStorage.setItem run synchronously on the browser main thread, allowing substantial CPU and memory consumption and potentially exhausting the origin's storage quota, causing subsequent saves to fail and degrading the chat UI. Browser quota provides only a hard failure boundary, not an application-level control against expensive serialization and parsing.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies an arbitrary StoredConversation object to the public save method; the TypeScript type does not impose a runtime size limit.

save loads the complete existing conversation collection and either replaces one item or appends the supplied object, so the serialized workload grows with both caller input and accumulated local data.
The entire collection is synchronously JSON-stringified and written to localStorage with no byte, message, or item-count cap, creating the resource-consumption sink.

title: Unbounded feedback collection request
description: `find` exposes the entire Feedbacks collection through a GET request while accepting optional query parameters without enforcing a page size or limit. A caller outside this file can invoke `find()` with no bounds, causing the backend to return an arbitrarily large collection if the API does not impose its own default pagination. Repeated requests can consume server memory, response bandwidth, and browser memory, degrading availability. The server-side default limit and infrastructure rate limits cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies optional query parameters to the exported `find` method; calling it with no parameters provides no client-enforced bounds.
The optional parameters are passed directly to the collection request without adding pagination, a maximum page size, or another result bound.
The unbounded collection GET is sent to `/api/Feedbacks/`, which can return an excessive result set if the server does not apply its own limit.

title: Unbounded order-history retrieval
description: The getAll method requests the entire order collection through /rest/order-history/orders without pagination parameters or a client-side bound. If the backing endpoint returns all records, an attacker who can repeatedly invoke this read operation can cause the server to query and serialize an arbitrarily large order set, while the browser must receive and materialize the full response through the response mapping. The server may have infrastructure-side limits, but no bound is evident in this service.

trace.description: The exported getAll method is callable by a caller outside this file and initiates retrieval of the order collection without accepting or imposing page, limit, or cursor parameters.
The response is passed through an unrestricted data extraction, preserving the complete returned collection for the caller.
The service sends a GET request to the collection endpoint /rest/order-history/orders with no pagination or result-size constraint visible in the request.

title: Unbounded photo-wall file upload
description: The photo-wall upload path accepts the caller-provided File and appends it directly to a multipart request without enforcing a maximum size or upload count. A caller outside this file can invoke addMemory with a very large file, causing the browser and the /rest/memories server endpoint to allocate and process the payload. If the server endpoint lacks an independent body-size limit, repeated large uploads can consume memory, bandwidth, temporary storage, and processing capacity, producing denial of service. The client-side check is not a sufficient security boundary, but this service visibly provides no upload-size control.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies an arbitrary caption and File to the exported service method.
The supplied File is appended to FormData without checking its size, type-related resource implications, or an upload count.
The unchecked multipart payload is sent to the memories API, allowing large payloads to reach the server endpoint.

title: Unbounded photo-wall collection retrieval
description: The get method requests the complete memories collection with no pagination, limit, or range parameter. A caller outside this file can repeatedly invoke it, and if the backing endpoint returns all stored memories, each response can consume client memory, network bandwidth, and server query/serialization resources in proportion to the collection size. The server may impose an independent limit, which cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and can invoke get to retrieve photo-wall memories.
The service constructs a collection request without page, offset, limit, or range controls.
The complete response data is requested from the memories collection endpoint and mapped into the client, potentially producing an unbounded result set.

title: Patch forwards caller-supplied review properties without a runtime allow-list
description: The patch method forwards the complete runtime review object to the backend. Although the static type lists only id and message, TypeScript types are not runtime allow-lists, so a caller can invoke the method with additional properties such as author, ownership, moderation, or other model fields. If the backend update endpoint binds request properties directly, this permits unauthorized modification of those properties. The backend persistence behavior is outside this file, so exploitability is conditional on that endpoint's binding behavior.

trace.description: A caller outside this file supplies the review object to the exported patch method. The compile-time type does not remove extra properties from a runtime object.
The complete review object is passed unchanged as the PATCH request body, with no runtime property filtering or explicit serialization allow-list.

title: Review authorship is client-controlled
description: The client accepts the review author as caller-controlled input and sends it to the review creation endpoint. A user can alter the request or call this method with another username, causing the server to attribute a review to an identity selected by the client if the backend trusts this field. Authorship should be derived from the authenticated session on the server rather than accepted as a client assertion.

trace.description: A caller outside this file supplies both message and author to the create method; the caller can choose the author value independently of the authenticated identity.
The client sends the supplied author directly in the review-creation request body, rather than obtaining authorship from a server-side identity context.

title: Product review listing requests an unbounded result set
description: The review listing request has no pagination, maximum page size, or client-side response bound. A product with a sufficiently large review collection can cause the endpoint and browser to transfer and materialize an unnecessarily large response in one request, creating memory, bandwidth, and processing pressure. The absence of server-side limits cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: A caller outside this file requests reviews for a product through get(id). The method provides no page, limit, or maximum-results argument.
The service issues a single GET request for the product's entire review collection and maps the full response, with no pagination or response-size control.

title: Unbounded retrieval of the Quantitys collection
description: QuantityService.getAll requests the entire Quantitys collection through a single unbounded collection request. The method supplies no page, limit, filter, or other bound, so a caller outside this file can repeatedly invoke it and cause the server to produce and the client to process an arbitrarily large result set. If the backing collection grows substantially, one request can consume server serialization/database resources and browser memory, degrading availability. Server-side pagination or a hard maximum response size is not visible here.

trace.description: Caller code outside this file can invoke the exported getAll method, which represents the attacker-reachable client-side entry to the collection retrieval operation.
getAll constructs a request to the collection URL without accepting or applying pagination, filtering, or a maximum item count.
Angular HttpClient performs the unbounded GET and maps the complete response data, causing the full result set to be returned and processed in memory.

title: Unbounded recycle collection retrieval
description: The exported find method receives caller-supplied query parameters from outside this file and sends a collection request to /api/Recycles without enforcing a page size, limit, or pagination contract. An attacker who can reach a caller of this service and cause repeated or broad list requests may cause the backend and client to process an arbitrarily large recycle result set, consuming database, network, server memory, and browser memory. The backend may provide independent pagination or infrastructure limits, which cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported find method accepts optional caller-controlled query parameters.
The arbitrary params object is forwarded directly as HTTP query parameters, with no enforced limit, page size, or pagination requirement.
HttpClient performs a collection GET against /api/Recycles/, which can return an unbounded result set when no server-side bound is applied.

title: Client-controlled X-User-Email header can enable identity spoofing
description: The interceptor accepts an email identity from browser-controlled localStorage and automatically sends it as X-User-Email on outgoing requests. A caller can modify localStorage before issuing a request, causing the interceptor to present an arbitrary user's email. If any backend authorization, ownership lookup, audit decision, or account operation trusts this header instead of deriving identity from the validated bearer token, User A can act as or access data belonging to User B by setting the header to User B's email. The downstream endpoint is outside this file, so the exact impact depends on whether the server trusts this header; the client-side trust violation is directly visible here.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies an HttpRequest to the interceptor; this is the entrypoint for the request transformation.

The interceptor reads the purported user identity from localStorage, which is browser-controlled and can be changed by the caller; there is no comparison with the bearer token or other integrity check.
The attacker-controlled email is copied into the X-User-Email header, creating a caller-supplied identity assertion.
The modified request is sent to the backend. Any downstream authorization logic that trusts X-User-Email receives the spoofed identity.

title: Password change sends credentials in a GET URL
description: The UserService password-change path receives password values from a caller outside this spec at line 94 and the test verifies that the service sends them as URL query parameters in a GET request at lines 96-99. Query URLs may be retained in browser history, intermediary/access logs, monitoring systems, caches, and referrer data. Using GET for a password mutation also permits unintended or cross-site triggering of the state change. An attacker or observer who obtains URL data may recover the current or replacement password, and a third party may cause the browser to issue the mutation without an explicit form submission.

trace.description: The caller, outside this file, supplies current and replacement password values to UserService.changePassword; this test invokes that externally callable service method with those values.
The service request is expected to encode current, new, and repeat password values directly into the URL query string.
The test confirms the security-sensitive password mutation uses HTTP GET, a cacheable and triggerable method, with credentials in the request URL.

title: OAuth access token exposed in URL query string
description: The OAuth login path receives an access token from a caller outside this file at line 182 and the test verifies that the token is appended to Google's URL as the access_token query parameter at line 184. URL query parameters are commonly exposed through browser history, proxy/server logs, analytics, caches, and referrer propagation. Anyone obtaining those records may replay the bearer token until it expires or is revoked, potentially accessing the user's Google profile data.

trace.description: The caller, outside this file, provides the OAuth bearer token to UserService.oauthLogin.
The service constructs the external Google user-info request with the caller-provided token as access_token in the URL.
The HTTP GET sends the bearer token in the request URL, exposing it to URL-based logging, history, caching, and referrer mechanisms.

title: Password change sends credentials in the URL
description: The exported changePassword method receives password values from a caller outside this file and sends the current and new passwords as URL query parameters in an HTTP GET request. URLs are commonly retained in browser history, reverse-proxy/access logs, monitoring systems, and intermediary request metadata. An attacker who obtains such URL data may recover the user's password material, including the new password, and potentially authenticate as the user or compromise other accounts where the password is reused. Password-changing operations should use a protected POST/PUT request body and avoid exposing credentials in URLs.

trace.description: Entrypoint: changePassword(passwords) is called by code outside this file and receives current, new, and repeat password values.
The caller-controlled password fields are concatenated into the request URL as query parameters.
HttpClient issues a GET request whose URL contains the current and new passwords, exposing them to URL handling and request logging infrastructure.

title: OAuth access token exposed in URL query string
description: The exported oauthLogin method accepts an access token from a caller outside this file and appends it to the Google userinfo URL as the access_token query parameter. Query-string tokens can leak through browser history, proxy/server logs, analytics, referrer-related metadata, and copied URLs. Anyone obtaining the token may use it until expiration or revocation to access the associated OAuth account or user information.

trace.description: Entrypoint: oauthLogin(accessToken) is called by code outside this file and receives an OAuth bearer access token.
The caller-controlled access token is interpolated into the Google userinfo request URL.
HttpClient sends the bearer token as the access_token query parameter, making it vulnerable to URL-based disclosure.

title: Unsanitized feedback comment is explicitly trusted as HTML
description: Feedback returned by feedbackService.find() is attacker-influenced data received from a caller/service outside this file. The component embeds each feedback comment directly into an HTML fragment and then marks the result as trusted with bypassSecurityTrustHtml. No context-appropriate sanitization or allowlist is applied before the trust bypass. The trusted fragment is passed to the gallery as args, where the gallery's HTML-rendering path can interpret attacker-supplied markup. A stored or reflected payload such as an event-handler attribute or other executable HTML, if accepted by the feedback backend, could execute in users' browsers when the About page gallery displays the feedback.

trace.description: The component receives the result of feedbackService.find(); the service/backend caller and the attacker-facing feedback submission path are outside this file.
For each returned feedback item, the comment value is interpolated into a figcaption HTML string. The comment is not encoded or otherwise constrained before being inserted into the fragment.

The constructed HTML fragment, including the externally returned comment, is passed directly to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml, explicitly disabling Angular's normal HTML sanitization for this value.
The trusted HTML value is supplied as the gallery image's args field, handing attacker-controlled markup to the gallery rendering path.

title: Client-controlled address ID used for edit without visible ownership authorization
description: The edit flow accepts an addressId from the client-controlled route and uses it to retrieve and update an address. The component performs no check that the address belongs to the authenticated user or that the user is authorized to modify it. An attacker can alter the route identifier to another address and the component will call the corresponding service methods. Whether the backend independently enforces ownership cannot be confirmed from this file, so this is a client-side authorization gap with moderate confidence rather than a confirmed server-side BOLA.

trace.description: The caller/router is outside this file; the component receives route parameters through ActivatedRoute.paramMap and subscribes to them.
When the route contains addressId, the component copies the caller-supplied identifier into addressId and enters edit mode.
The selected identifier is passed to AddressService.getById without a per-user ownership check in this component.
On save, the same route-derived identifier and the edited address data are sent to AddressService.put; no authorization or ownership check occurs between identifier selection and mutation.

title: Unbounded loading of accounting collections into browser memory
description: When the component initializes, it requests the complete quantity collection, an unfiltered product search, and the complete order history. The results are assigned to arrays and wrapped in MatTableDataSource instances, with no pagination parameter, maximum-result argument, or client-side cap visible in this file. An attacker who can repeatedly reach the accounting component can trigger requests whose response and browser memory usage grow with the total inventory, product, or order-history size; in particular, getAll() for order history can become an unbounded result-set operation unless a limit is enforced elsewhere by the service or API.

trace.description: Angular invokes ngAfterViewInit when the component is initialized; the caller/framework entrypoint is outside this file.
Initialization starts loading all inventory quantities through loadQuantity().
loadQuantity calls quantityService.getAll() without a page size or result limit.
Initialization starts loading products through loadProducts(), which uses an empty search term rather than a bounded query.
loadProducts calls productService.search('') without pagination or a maximum-result argument.
Initialization starts loading order history through loadOrders().
loadOrders calls orderHistoryService.getAll() without pagination or a result limit, creating the unbounded collection-fetch path.

title: Address deletion forwards caller-supplied ID without visible ownership enforcement
description: The address deletion path accepts an arbitrary numeric identifier and immediately passes it to AddressService.del(id), with no per-resource ownership or authorization check in this component. A caller able to invoke this method or trigger the corresponding UI action with another address's ID can request deletion of that record. Because the actual service implementation and backend authorization are outside this file, exploitability depends on whether the server independently enforces ownership; client-side selection alone is not a sufficient authorization boundary.

trace.description: The component receives an address ID through deleteAddress(id); its caller is outside this source file (for example, the component template or another component). No authenticated-user or ownership context is checked here.
The supplied ID is propagated unchanged to AddressService.del(id). There is no validation or comparison against the component's loaded addresses or current user between method entry and this call.

AddressService.del(id) is the deletion sink. If the service/backend accepts the identifier without server-side per-address authorization, substituting another user's address ID enables unauthorized deletion.

title: Stored client-side XSS through bypassSecurityTrustHtml
description: The component receives user emails and feedback comments from service/API responses and explicitly marks them as trusted HTML. Angular's normal sanitization is bypassed at lines 73 and 91. If an attacker can submit or influence an email or feedback comment, payloads such as closing tags followed by an event-bearing element can execute when the administration table renders the trusted value. This is especially impactful because the affected view exposes administrative data and actions.

trace.description: The users callback receives data returned by the UserService; the service/API caller is outside this file.
The returned user.email is interpolated into an HTML string and passed to bypassSecurityTrustHtml, disabling Angular sanitization for attacker-influenced content.
The feedback callback similarly receives externally supplied feedback records and assigns the comment value for display.
feedback.comment is explicitly marked as trusted HTML without sanitization, making attacker-controlled markup executable when the consuming template renders it as HTML.

title: Unbounded administrative list loading before client-side pagination
description: Both administrative list loaders retrieve and retain the complete result set in memory. The paginator is attached after the full array has already been returned and wrapped in MatTableDataSource, so it provides client-side presentation pagination rather than limiting the service/API response. If the underlying collections grow large or an attacker can create many records, a single administration-page load can cause excessive response transfer, browser memory use, and table-processing work. The file shows no page, limit, or server-side pagination parameter.

trace.description: findAllUsers invokes UserService.find(); the service and its server-side request behavior are outside this file, and no pagination or limit is passed by this component.
The complete users collection is assigned directly to component state.
The full collection is wrapped in MatTableDataSource and only then assigned a paginator, meaning pagination occurs after retrieval and materialization.
findAllFeedbacks makes the same unbounded find() call for feedback records, with no page or result cap supplied.
The complete feedback collection is materialized into MatTableDataSource and its total length is computed before display pagination, consuming resources proportional to the entire response.

title: Sensitive account routes lack authentication guards
description: Several account- and payment-related UI routes are reachable without an Angular authentication or authorization guard. In particular, an unauthenticated user can directly request /saved-payment-methods and /privacy-security/data-export instead of being redirected by LoginGuard. This bypasses the frontend's stated access-control pattern: nearby address routes use LoginGuard, while these sensitive routes do not. The route guard is not a substitute for server-side authorization, so backend APIs may still prevent data access; however, if these components or their APIs rely on the route gate, an attacker can directly initialize the components and invoke their associated operations without first authenticating through the application flow.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint: a caller outside this file can navigate directly to the Angular path /saved-payment-methods.
The route configuration also exposes the account-security parent route without canActivate; its child routes include change-password, two-factor-authentication, data-export, and last-login-ip.
The sensitive data-export component is reachable as a child route and no LoginGuard or role guard is configured before it is activated.

title: Administrative route authorization trusts an unverified JWT role claim
description: The admin route guard authorizes navigation using payload.data.role from a JWT that was only decoded, not cryptographically verified. The caller of AdminGuard.canActivate is outside this file; once invoked during route activation, it reads the token from localStorage, parses attacker-controlled JWT contents with jwtDecode, and accepts the route when the payload claims the admin role. An attacker can place a forged token containing data.role equal to roles.admin in localStorage and pass this client-side privilege check. Any sensitive operation must still be protected server-side, but this guard is not a trustworthy authorization boundary and can expose administrative UI or enable requests made without an independent server authorization check.

trace.description: The router/framework caller is outside this file and invokes AdminGuard.canActivate during navigation.
AdminGuard obtains the token payload through LoginGuard.tokenDecode().
tokenDecode reads the browser-local token and passes it to jwtDecode, which parses claims without signature verification or expiration enforcement in this code path.
The guard treats the decoded, unverified data.role claim as sufficient proof of administrative authorization and allows navigation.

title: Login guard authenticates based only on token presence
description: LoginGuard considers a route authenticated whenever localStorage contains a non-empty value named token. It does not validate that the value is a JWT, verify a signature, check expiry, or establish the identity represented by the token. A caller outside this file triggers canActivate during route navigation; an attacker controlling their browser can insert any non-empty string into localStorage and the guard returns true, bypassing this client-side authentication gate. This is not a substitute for server-side authentication and authorization, and any route relying on this guard alone is exposed to unauthorized client-side access.

trace.description: The Angular router/framework caller is outside this file and invokes LoginGuard.canActivate for a protected route.
The guard reads localStorage and uses only the truthiness of the token value as its authentication decision; no token validation or identity verification occurs.
Any non-empty localStorage token causes the guard to return true, allowing navigation without cryptographic authentication or an authorization decision.

title: Privileged password policy is advisory and based on client-controlled identity
description: The component attempts to enforce a stronger password policy for accounts whose email matches the support pattern, but the policy check is advisory: it emits a console message and then unconditionally invokes UserService.changePassword. An attacker can also alter the localStorage email value used by the check, so the client cannot reliably determine whether the account is privileged. If the backend relies on this client-side control, a weak password can be submitted for a privileged support account by selecting a nonmatching or forged localStorage email, or simply by proceeding after the warning. The server must derive the account identity and enforce the policy; the client should not treat this check as the control that protects the account.

trace.description: The change-password workflow is entered through the component's public changePassword method; its caller and the authenticated account context are outside this file.

The component decides whether the account is a privileged support account using the email stored in browser-controlled localStorage, which an attacker can modify independently of the server-side account identity.
When the new password fails the stronger policy, the component only calls console.error and does not return, disable submission, or otherwise reject the operation.

Regardless of the policy result, the component sends the current, new, and repeated passwords to UserService.changePassword, allowing the client-side policy to be bypassed if it is the only enforcement point.

title: Unbounded socket-driven notification and progress-request amplification
description: The socket handler accepts runtime data from outside this file and performs no rate limiting, deduplication, queue bound, or payload validation. For every event with a truthy challenge, visible events are appended to the notifications array, which has no maximum size. The same event also invokes saveProgress for every non-restore notification, causing a separate continueCode service request. An attacker able to cause or inject repeated qualifying socket events can therefore grow the browser's notification state without bound and amplify requests to the progress endpoint, degrading the victim's browser and potentially the backend.

trace.description: The component receives the `challenge solved` socket event and its runtime `data` object from a caller outside this file; the TypeScript interface does not perform runtime validation.
Only a truthy `data.challenge` is required before processing; for non-hidden events the externally supplied object is passed into notification creation.
Each processed notification is pushed into `notifications` with no size limit, duplicate suppression, or backpressure. Repeated events can grow this client-side array indefinitely.
Independently, every non-restore qualifying event invokes `saveProgress`, with no per-event throttling or deduplication.
`saveProgress` starts a `continueCode()` service request for each event, creating request amplification when the socket event is repeated.

title: Unbounded chat input, history, and streamed response consumption
description: The chat request path has no application-level bounds on either user input or accumulated conversation/output. sendMessage accepts any non-empty string (lines 114-115), appends it to the in-memory history (line 117), and then serializes every retained non-error message into apiMessages (lines 126-129) before calling the chat backend (line 131). The streamed response is appended indefinitely to the assistant message at lines 146-152, with no maximum output length or timeout. A caller outside this file can also place an arbitrary initialMessage in the URL; ngOnInit automatically invokes sendMessage at lines 77-80. An attacker can cause a victim to load such a URL, or repeatedly submit very large messages, producing oversized API requests, expensive model processing, and unbounded browser memory/local-storage growth. Server-side limits may mitigate backend impact, but no such control is present in this component.

trace.description: An attacker-controlled URL query parameter can enter this component as initialMessage; the caller/navigation source is outside this file.
The component automatically submits the arbitrary query value without an explicit user action, and sendMessage also accepts arbitrary caller-provided content.
sendMessage only rejects an empty string or a currently loading request; it applies no length or payload-size limit before appending content to the conversation.
The complete accumulated conversation is mapped into apiMessages, so repeated or very large messages cause request size and model-processing cost to grow without a history bound.
The unbounded apiMessages array is submitted to the chat streaming service without a client-side size, rate, or timeout control.
Every streamed delta is concatenated into the assistant message without a maximum response size, allowing unbounded client-side memory growth.

title: Raw configuration errors exposed through browser-console logging
description: When application configuration loading fails, the component logs the complete error object directly to the browser console. Depending on the HTTP client and server response, this object may include request URLs, status details, response bodies, or diagnostic error traces. Browser-console output is visible to the user and may be collected by browser extensions or client-side telemetry, while this unstructured logging does not provide reliable centralized monitoring or correlation for configuration failures. An attacker able to trigger or induce a configuration failure could cause internal diagnostic details to be exposed to the client, reducing the application's ability to safely investigate the event.

trace.description: The component invokes the externally implemented application-configuration service; the service and its HTTP response/error generation are outside this file.
The error value from the configuration request is passed unchanged into a console logging call.

title: Continuation code cookie lacks transport and cross-site protections
description: When the verdict is true, the helper obtains a server-issued continuation code and stores it in a browser cookie. The cookie configuration explicitly supplies only an expiration date one year in the future and omits security attributes such as Secure and SameSite. If the application is reachable over HTTP or the browser makes cross-site requests, the continuation code can be exposed over an unencrypted connection or sent in cross-site requests, potentially allowing an attacker to replay the code and continue the challenge workflow. The code is also written by client-side JavaScript, so HttpOnly protection cannot be applied through this API.

trace.description: The exported helper receives the verdict and service dependencies from a caller outside this file; the caller can trigger this path when a challenge verdict is considered correct.
For a true verdict, the helper invokes the appropriate continuation-code request and subscribes to the returned server value.

The server-provided continueCode is written to a browser cookie with a one-year expiration, but no Secure or SameSite attributes are supplied, leaving the token subject to weaker browser transport and cross-site handling.

title: Unsanitized export data written into a browser document
description: The data export response is treated as HTML and written directly into a new browser document. The component receives the response from the data export service, assigns its userData field without validation or sanitization, and passes it to document.write. If an attacker can cause exported data or another returned field to contain HTML/script markup, that markup executes in the newly opened same-origin window. This can enable DOM XSS in the application's origin, including theft of accessible application data or actions performed with the user's browser session.

trace.description: The caller and backend response source are outside this file; the component receives the asynchronous data export response in the service subscription callback.
The response's userData field is copied directly into component state without an allowlist, context-appropriate encoding, or sanitization.
The dynamic userData value is inserted into a newly opened document using document.write, which interprets the value as HTML and can execute attacker-controlled markup or script.

title: Client-controlled UserId permits feedback misattribution
description: The component obtains the current user's ID, places it in a mutable userIdControl, and later copies that control's value into the UserId property of the feedback object. Because the value is controlled in the browser, an attacker can alter the submitted request and attribute feedback to another user's ID. The server-side feedback endpoint must derive the owner from the authenticated session and reject or ignore caller-supplied UserId; that enforcement is not present in this client-side flow. This can corrupt user attribution and may enable actions or views that trust the feedback owner's identity.

The returned identity is copied into the feedback model and a client-side control: this.feedback.UserId = data.id and this.userIdControl.setValue(data.id). The control is a browser-side value and is not a trusted authorization boundary.
On save, the component overwrites the model's owner field with the current value of the mutable userIdControl, allowing a modified client or forged request to substitute another user's identifier.
The feedback object, including the caller-selected UserId property, is submitted to the feedback API through the service. No ownership check or server-derived identity is visible in this file.

title: Client-controlled address identifier passed to lookup without visible ownership enforcement
description: During initialization, the component obtains the target address identifier from sessionStorage, which is fully modifiable by the browser user, and sends it to AddressService.getById(). There is no ownership check in this component tying the address to the authenticated user. If the corresponding API or service also performs an unscoped lookup, User A can replace addressId with User B's address identifier and retrieve/display User B's address. The actual server-side authorization check cannot be confirmed from this file.

The component reads addressId directly from sessionStorage, a browser-controlled value, and supplies it as the resource identifier to the address service.
AddressService.getById() is the lookup sink. No per-user ownership or authorization check occurs in this component before the returned address is assigned for display.

title: Client-controlled delivery method state carried into payment workflow
description: The component treats a client-controlled delivery method identifier as sufficient state for advancing to payment: it writes deliveryMethodId into sessionStorage and immediately navigates to the payment flow. A user can modify sessionStorage or invoke the handler with an arbitrary identifier before payment. If downstream order/payment logic trusts this identifier or derives price/ETA from client-selected state rather than revalidating the allowed method and authoritative price server-side, the workflow can be subverted, potentially producing an unauthorized delivery choice or economic impact. Downstream validation is not visible in this file.

The selected identifier is serialized into sessionStorage, which the browser user can freely alter before the next workflow step.
The component advances directly to the payment route after persisting the client-controlled identifier; no server-side revalidation or re-derivation is visible here.

title: Wallet chain-change listeners accumulate without cleanup
description: Each initialization of FaucetComponent registers a new chainChanged handler with the injected wallet provider. The component has no ngOnDestroy method or other removal of that handler. If the route/component is created repeatedly, old handlers remain registered; one subsequent chain change invokes handleChainChanged once per accumulated instance, causing repeated wallet reconnects and balance RPC calls. This can grow client memory and amplify RPC/provider work, degrading the user's browser and potentially generating excessive provider traffic.

A chainChanged callback is registered on window.ethereum, but no corresponding listener removal or component-destruction cleanup exists in this file.

title: Untrusted JWT data passed through Angular HTML sanitizer bypass
description: The component takes the `lastLoginIp` field from a JWT stored in browser localStorage and constructs an HTML fragment containing that value. It then calls Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly disabling Angular's normal HTML sanitization. If an attacker can influence the token payload or the stored token through an existing client-side compromise or an attacker-controlled server-issued claim, a value such as `">` can be interpreted as HTML when the component template renders `lastLoginIp`, potentially executing script in the application's origin. The component performs no validation or context-appropriate sanitization before the bypass.

The token is decoded client-side and the `payload.data.lastLoginIp` field is copied into component state without validation or sanitization.

The dynamic field is interpolated into an HTML string and passed to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, disabling Angular's sanitization. When the resulting trusted value is bound by the component template, attacker-supplied markup such as an event-handler payload can execute in the application's origin.

title: Forgot-password flow permits account enumeration through security-question disclosure
description: The forgot-password UI exposes account existence through the security-question lookup. When the externally supplied email produces a question, the component assigns that question to client-visible state and enables the password-reset controls; when no question is returned, those controls are disabled. An attacker can submit candidate email addresses and distinguish registered accounts from unregistered ones based on the response/UI state. This leaks account enumeration information and also discloses the recovery question to anyone who knows an account email, weakening the password-reset design.

The component reads the externally supplied email value and sends it to SecurityQuestionService.findBy after the timeout.

A truthy lookup result is copied into component state as the security question, while the absence of a result disables the recovery controls, creating an observable registered-versus-unregistered distinction.

title: Forgot-password lookup lacks effective request throttling in the client flow
description: The component issues a security-question lookup for each email edit after a one-second debounce, but the debounce only delays pending calls. It does not impose a rate limit, cancel an already-running request, or prevent repeated requests. An attacker can repeatedly trigger the handler with different email values or invoke the underlying API directly, generating an unbounded stream of password-recovery lookups. Backend or infrastructure throttling is not visible in this file, so the effectiveness and severity of external controls cannot be confirmed.

title: Login flow trusts redirectUrl query parameter without demonstrated destination validation
description: The test explicitly verifies that the login flow forwards the value obtained from the redirectUrl query parameter directly to router.navigateByUrl. If the production component does not constrain this value to approved same-origin application routes, an attacker can send a victim a login URL containing an attacker-controlled redirect target and cause navigation there after authentication. This can enable phishing and, depending on the redirect mechanism and target handling, token or authorization-code exposure. The actual component implementation is outside this file, so the absence of validation cannot be confirmed here; the test demonstrates that arbitrary redirect forwarding is an intended behavior.

The test asserts that the component navigates directly to the supplied redirect target using navigateByUrl, without any visible allowlist, same-origin check, or path validation in this file.

title: OAuth login request lacks state validation and uses the implicit token flow
description: The Google OAuth authorization request is constructed without a state parameter and uses response_type=token. Because the authorization response cannot be correlated to a login attempt initiated by this browser, an attacker can induce a victim to visit an authorization URL or callback containing the attacker's OAuth token. If the application's callback accepts that token, the victim can be logged into the attacker's account (login CSRF/account confusion), potentially causing the victim to submit sensitive data to the wrong account. The implicit flow also places the access token in the browser redirect fragment and should not be used for modern OAuth authorization.

title: Hardcoded testing credentials exposed in the frontend bundle
description: Plaintext credentials for the testing account are embedded in public component properties. Angular frontend code is delivered to users, so an attacker can inspect the source or compiled JavaScript and obtain testing@juice-sh.op / IamUsedForTesting, then authenticate as that account wherever the account remains enabled. Credentials must not be shipped in client code, even if intended only for testing.

title: OAuth accounts receive predictable reversible passwords derived from email addresses
description: The OAuth fallback account flow is specified to create a normal account with `password` equal to a Base64 encoding of the reversed email address (for example, `test@test.com` becomes `bW9jLnRzZXRAdHNldA==`). Base64 is reversible and provides no password hashing, salting, or secret entropy. The same spec also requires that this predictable value be supplied to the regular login flow when account creation fails because the account already exists. An attacker who knows an email address can compute the password and attempt regular authentication. This file is a test specification rather than the production implementation, so the finding is based on the insecure behavior it explicitly locks in; the production calls are implemented by OAuthComponent outside this file.

The test asserts that account creation receives the email together with a password and passwordRepeat equal to the reversible Base64-encoded reversed email value.
A second scenario models an existing account by making account creation fail after receiving the same OAuth email.
The component is invoked again through the OAuth initialization path, causing its existing-account fallback behavior to run.
The spec asserts that the predictable derived password is then used for regular login, confirming the credential is intended to be a usable authentication secret.

title: Arbitrary order identifier trusted without ownership enforcement
description: The component treats the route parameter as sufficient authority to retrieve and display an order. A caller outside this file supplies the route id; the component passes that identifier to TrackOrderService.find and renders the returned order without checking that it belongs to the current user. It also uses the returned addressId for a separate address lookup and constructs a PDF URL from the same unverified order id. If the corresponding order and PDF API endpoints do not enforce ownership server-side, User A can substitute User B's order id and obtain B's order details, address information, and confirmation PDF. The client-side component provides no compensating authorization control.

The same unverified route orderId is embedded in a PDF URL and opened, potentially exposing another user's order confirmation if the backing resource does not independently enforce authorization.

title: Order PDF opened without an observable ownership check
description: The component exposes an order-specific PDF operation that trusts the supplied orderId and directly opens the corresponding FTP resource. There is no ownership or authorization check in this code between receiving the identifier and using it. If the backing FTP/static resource does not independently enforce the authenticated user's order ownership, User A can invoke this handler with User B's orderId and retrieve User B's PDF, potentially exposing order history and other personal data. title: OAuth accounts receive passwords deterministically derived from email addresses
description: The OAuth flow derives the user's password as Base64(reverse(email)). Base64 is encoding rather than password protection, and the resulting password is deterministic and recoverable by anyone who knows the account email. The value is persisted through the account-save operation and then submitted to the normal login operation. An attacker who knows an OAuth user's email can calculate the same password and authenticate through the regular login path without completing the OAuth identity-verification flow, depending on the server's normal login behavior.

title: Authentication token is stored without explicit cookie transport protections
description: The component stores the bearer authentication token in a client-managed cookie while specifying only an expiry. No Secure or SameSite attributes are requested, so if the application is reachable over HTTP the token can be transmitted in cleartext, and cookie cross-site protections are not established by this code. The token is also copied to localStorage, making it available to any script executing in the origin and providing a persistent bearer-token target.

The login response supplies authentication.token and authentication.bid to the client.

The same bearer token is stored in localStorage, where JavaScript running in the origin can read it and reuse it for authenticated requests.

title: Authentication token persisted in JavaScript-accessible browser storage
description: The deluxe upgrade response supplies an authentication token, and the component persists that token in browser local storage and through the cookie service. The local-storage write makes the bearer token readable by any JavaScript executing in the application's origin; an XSS or compromised third-party script can steal it and replay it to impersonate the user. The cookie write is also performed without any security options visible at this call site, although the cookie service's defaults cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: String control values bypass MIME-type validation
description: This validator accepts every string-valued control without inspecting its contents. An attacker who can provide or preserve a string value can cause the validator to return null, the Angular validation-success result, without reading or checking file bytes. If the caller uses this result as the upload acceptance gate, the attacker can bypass the intended MIME/signature check by submitting a string or otherwise invoking the upload path directly; server-side validation is required because this client-side control is attacker-manipulable. The downstream caller and server enforcement are outside this file, so the impact depends on whether they independently validate the upload.

The validator branches solely on whether control.value is a string. It does not verify that the string represents an approved file, URL, or server-validated asset.

title: Client-controlled basket ID used without visible ownership enforcement
description: applyCoupon takes the basket identifier from browser-controlled sessionStorage and passes it directly to the basket service. There is no ownership or authorization check in this component between receiving the identifier and issuing the operation. If the corresponding endpoint authorizes only by the supplied basket ID, an authenticated user could replace bid with another user's basket ID and apply a coupon to that basket. Server-side scoping may mitigate this, so the finding is based on the visible client-side authorization gap.

The client-controlled bid is supplied to basketService.applyCoupon, with no per-basket ownership check visible in this component.

title: Authentication bearer token persisted in script-readable localStorage
description: After a deluxe upgrade, the component stores the returned authentication token in localStorage and also writes it to a cookie. localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript executing in the origin, so a later XSS or compromised third-party script can exfiltrate the bearer token and impersonate the user. The file does not show an HttpOnly-only storage strategy or secure cookie attributes.

title: Wallet charge amount is trusted from client-side session state
description: The wallet charging request uses this.totalPrice, which is calculated from values held in sessionStorage. In wallet mode, walletTotal is parsed directly from sessionStorage and becomes totalPrice; the value is then sent as the balance in a wallet mutation. An attacker can modify walletTotal in browser developer tools before completing payment and cause the client to submit an attacker-chosen amount. The server must independently derive and validate the payable amount, but no such trusted derivation is visible in this component.

For wallet mode, the payment total is taken directly from browser-controlled sessionStorage without a server-side quote or integrity check.
The locally derived totalPrice is sent as the balance in the wallet mutation request.

title: Unbounded image file is fully buffered for preview and upload
description: The image-picker handler accepts the selected File without a size limit. It immediately reads the entire file into memory as a base64 data URL for preview, and save() later forwards the original file to the upload service. An attacker who can use this UI can select or automate submission of an unusually large file, causing substantial browser memory allocation from FileReader and potentially generating an oversized upload request. The component has no visible client-side size cap; server-side enforcement may mitigate the upload leg but does not prevent the preview memory exhaustion.

The handler obtains the first externally selected File and places it directly into the form without checking its size, dimensions, or byte count.
The FileReader is configured to read the entire file as a data URL, causing memory use proportional to the complete file size and adding base64 expansion.
The unchecked File value is passed to the memory-upload service when the form is saved; no size limit is enforced in this component before the upload operation.

title: Client-controlled review author identity
description: The review payload explicitly includes `author: this.author` and sends it to the review creation service. `this.author` is populated from a client-side component property after a `whoAmI` response, but browser-side state and the request body are fully attacker-modifiable. If the review API persists the supplied author instead of deriving the author from the authenticated session, any logged-in user can submit reviews impersonating another email address (or alter the value before submission). This is a trust-boundary design flaw: authorship, an integrity-sensitive fact, is accepted from the client rather than being server-authoritative. The server-side review handler must derive the author from the authenticated principal and ignore or reject the client-supplied field.

The component stores the current identity in the mutable client-side `author` property based on the `whoAmI` response; this value can be changed by an attacker through browser manipulation before submission.
The mutable client-side identity is copied into the review request body as the `author` field.

The review object, including the client-supplied author, is submitted to the review creation service. The component provides no server-authoritative identity binding or client-side integrity protection.

title: Client-controlled basket ID enables potential cross-user basket access
description: The authenticated add-to-basket flow trusts the basket ID stored in browser sessionStorage. A caller can modify the `bid` value before invoking this component's flow. The component then requests that basket with `basketService.find(...)` and, when the product is absent, submits a new item whose `BasketId` is the same attacker-selected value. There is no client-side ownership check tying the basket to the authenticated user. If the corresponding backend operations do not independently enforce basket ownership, User A can read or modify User B's basket by replacing `sessionStorage.bid` with User B's basket ID. The client-side `isLoggedIn` input is also not a security boundary; authorization must be enforced server-side.

For the logged-in branch, the component reads `bid` directly from mutable browser sessionStorage and converts it to the identifier passed to the basket lookup. No ownership or user-to-basket binding is checked in this file.

If the selected product is not already present, the same sessionStorage-derived basket identifier is copied into the object submitted as `BasketId`; this is an explicit client-controlled resource reference rather than a value derived from trusted identity.

The basket item is persisted through `basketService.save(...)` using the attacker-selected `BasketId`. Without a server-side ownership check, substituting another user's basket ID permits cross-user basket modification.

title: Client-controlled recycle ownership identifier

The component initially obtains the ID from whoAmI, but stores it in the mutable public `recycle` object and sends that object to the API. An attacker controlling their browser or intercepting the request can replace UserId with another user's ID. If the POST /api/Recycles handler trusts this field instead of deriving ownership from the authenticated session, the attacker can create recycle records attributed to another user and potentially affect that user's data or workflow. The backend authorization behavior is outside this file, so exploitability is contingent on that server-side trust.

The returned identity ID is copied into the mutable, any-typed recycle object as UserId. No immutable binding or server-derived ownership mechanism is visible here.
Additional client-side fields are added to the same object, while the UserId remains part of the object that will be submitted.

The entire mutable recycle object, including UserId, is sent to the recycle creation service. A caller can alter this field before or during the request unless the backend independently derives and authorizes ownership.

title: Weak five-character minimum password policy
description: The registration form explicitly permits passwords as short as five characters (line 51) and submits the value to the registration service (line 77). If the backend accepts the same policy, users can create accounts protected by low-entropy passwords that are substantially easier to brute-force or guess. Because this control is implemented in the client, it can also be bypassed by sending a direct request; a server-side minimum and stronger password policy are required for effective enforcement.

The permitted password value is included in the newly constructed registration object and sent to the user service for account creation.

title: Client-controlled basket ID is used without visible ownership enforcement
description: The basket lookup uses the basket ID stored in browser-controlled sessionStorage and does not perform a per-user ownership check before requesting the basket. A user can alter the bid value and cause this component to request another basket ID. If the corresponding backend lookup is not independently scoped to the authenticated user, User A can substitute User B's basket ID and read its products and totals. The component also exposes item IDs to mutation methods without a local authorization boundary, so server-side ownership enforcement is required.

title: Guest basket quantities are not bounded at a positive minimum

When a guest item has quantity 1, invoking dec() passes 0 to updateGuestBasketItemQuantity; repeated calls can produce negative quantities. The component subsequently multiplies prices by these quantities when calculating itemTotal at line 128. If guest basket data is later used by checkout or synchronized with the server without independent quantity validation, an attacker can create negative or otherwise invalid line items and potentially reduce the calculated purchase amount.

Because guest basket contents are browser-controlled, a manipulated or excessively large guest basket can create a large burst of HTTP requests and consume browser, network, and backend resources.

The component does not sanitize or validate the description before applying this bypass. If an attacker can create or modify a challenge description through the application's challenge-management functionality, malicious HTML or script-capable markup can be rendered by the associated challenge-card template, resulting in stored client-side XSS against users viewing the scoreboard. The template is referenced at line 41 and the actual rendering is outside this file, but the unsafe trust decision is visible here.

A payload such as a closing code tag followed by an event-bearing HTML element could alter the rendered DOM and may execute script in a context supported by the browser and template.

title: MFA bearer token stored without secure cookie protections

The handler builds a CSP header for the profile response after incorporating the user's profile data into the rendered page.
The response explicitly permits eval-like browser behavior through script-src 'unsafe-eval', weakening a key CSP mitigation against script injection.

title: Unauthenticated video streaming lacks rate limiting or resource controls
description: GET /video is publicly reachable and streams a potentially large video file. The handler accepts requests without any visible per-IP, per-user, per-route throttling or concurrency limit, and each request creates a filesystem read stream that is piped directly to the response. An attacker can issue many concurrent full-file or range requests to consume server disk I/O, file descriptors, response bandwidth, and upstream connection capacity, potentially degrading availability. Infrastructure-level rate limiting may mitigate this, but no such control is present in this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; this exported handler is registered as unauthenticated GET /video and receives the incoming request.
The handler reads the client-controlled Range header and uses it to create a separate filesystem stream for each request, with no request count, concurrency, or bandwidth limit.
For requests without a Range header, the entire video is streamed to the client; repeated or concurrent requests can consume disk and network resources without throttling.

title: Wallet top-up accepts negative or unbounded balance amounts
description: The PUT wallet-balance handler receives the balance amount from the request and passes it directly to WalletModel.increment without validating that it is a finite, non-negative top-up amount. Because the endpoint is designed to add wallet funds after card validation, an attacker can submit a negative balance (for example, -100). The ORM then applies that negative increment to the user's wallet, allowing the add-funds workflow to perform an unintended debit and potentially corrupt or manipulate wallet/accounting state. There is also no visible upper bound or numeric validation for excessively large values.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported addWalletBalance handler for PUT /rest/wallet/balance; request data is available through req.body.

The handler reads the caller-controlled paymentId and balance fields from req.body. Although it validates that the selected card belongs to req.body.UserId, it performs no validation of the balance amount itself.

After the card check succeeds, req.body.balance is supplied directly as the increment amount. Negative values therefore reduce the wallet despite this being an add-balance operation, and no finite or maximum-value check is applied.

title: Wallet balance mutations are not security-audited
description: This financial mutation path has no audit logging. Neither successful balance changes nor failures are recorded before the response is returned. If an account is abused or wallet balances are manipulated, this handler provides no event record containing the operation outcome, making detection and forensic reconstruction difficult.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported addWalletBalance handler for PUT /rest/wallet/balance, a security-relevant financial operation.
The handler validates card existence and ownership, then enters the wallet mutation path; no logger, audit service, correlation record, or monitoring hook is invoked in this flow.
The balance is changed by WalletModel.increment and the handler immediately returns success or a generic error. There is no logging of the amount, user, result, or failure.

title: Unauthenticated verdict endpoint lacks throttling for repeated filesystem and YAML work
description: POST /snippets/verdict is publicly reachable and the handler performs filesystem and YAML-processing work for every request. An attacker can repeatedly submit requests with a valid challenge key and selectedLines, causing repeated stat, file-read, YAML parsing, attempt tracking, and possibly challenge-solving operations. No per-IP, per-user, or per-endpoint rate limit or other throttling control is present in this handler. The impact is primarily increased CPU and filesystem load and possible service degradation; infrastructure-level limits, if configured elsewhere, cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives an unauthenticated POST request body containing the challenge key and selected lines.
The request-controlled key is read and used to retrieve challenge data, while selectedLines is later taken directly from the request body.
Each request performs a filesystem existence check and then reads and parses the corresponding YAML challenge metadata before returning a verdict.

title: Unauthenticated challenge-solving state change
description: The POST /snippets/fixes endpoint is reachable without authentication. Its caller-controlled key is passed to readFixes, and when the selected answer is correct the handler calls challengeUtils.solveFixIt(key). Thus an unauthenticated attacker can submit answers for arbitrary discovered challenge keys and cause challenge-solving state to be recorded without an authenticated user or authorization check. The finite answer space can also be tested because the endpoint returns a verdict and has no visible throttling.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the externally registered POST /snippets/fixes route invokes this exported handler without authentication middleware; the caller is outside this file.
The request body supplies key and selectedFix, and the key is used to load the corresponding fix data without any user or role check.
The selected answer is compared with the server-side correct index, but no authorization check is performed before the state-changing operation.
A correct unauthenticated request invokes challengeUtils.solveFixIt(key), recording the challenge as solved.

title: Path traversal in code-fix metadata lookup
description: The POST handler accepts an unrestricted body key and concatenates it into a filesystem path for the challenge-info YAML file. A key containing traversal segments can escape data/static/codefixes and cause the server to read another readable file whose name ends with .info.yml. The parsed explanation may then be returned to the attacker. No canonicalization, directory containment check, or allow-list is visible.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the externally supplied POST body is received by checkCorrectFix; the route caller is outside this file.
The attacker-controlled key is read directly from req.body and used in the metadata lookup path.
The key is concatenated into a relative filesystem path without validation or confinement to FixesDir.

The constructed path is read and parsed as YAML, allowing disclosure of attacker-selected readable files matching the .info.yml suffix and potentially exposing their explanation content in the response.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled code-fix cache
description: readFixes uses a plain process-global object as an unbounded cache keyed by arbitrary request input. For every new key, it scans the code-fixes directory and stores a new entry permanently. Because GET /snippets/fixes/:key has no authentication or visible rate limit, an attacker can issue requests with many unique keys, causing repeated filesystem work and unbounded memory growth. The plain-object lookup also treats inherited names such as __proto__ as cache entries, which can produce invalid values and repeated handler errors.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the unauthenticated GET /snippets/fixes/:key route passes an externally controlled path key into this handler; the route registration is outside this file.
The arbitrary route parameter is passed to readFixes on every request.
For cache misses, the function scans the directory and reads matching files, performing filesystem work for each unique attacker-supplied key.
Every unique key is retained indefinitely in the global CodeFixes object, with no size bound, expiry, eviction, or rate limit.

title: Unauthenticated access to global Web3 listener setup
description: The route is publicly reachable and has no authentication or authorization middleware, yet it performs a server-wide side effect: it records the caller-supplied wallet address and, when not already initialized, creates a blockchain WebSocket provider and contract event listener. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore invoke an operation that changes shared server state and initiates an external listener without demonstrating any authorization to do so. The lack of authorization also makes the listener setup available to arbitrary callers rather than a trusted application workflow.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; this exported handler is registered as POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress with no authentication middleware, so an anonymous caller can enter the operation.
The handler accepts the caller-controlled walletAddress and mutates the process-global walletsConnected Set before any authorization or validation check.
The handler conditionally constructs a WebSocketProvider and Contract listener using shared server resources, then marks the global listener as created.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled wallet Set and listener initialization
description: The unauthenticated endpoint allows an attacker to submit unlimited distinct walletAddress values. Each value is retained in the process-global walletsConnected Set and is removed only if a matching ContractExploited event later occurs. There is no input validation, maximum Set size, expiration, cleanup policy, or route-level rate limit. Repeated requests with unique values can therefore grow server memory without bound. Additionally, concurrent requests can all observe isEventListenerCreated as false before the asynchronous provider setup completes, potentially creating multiple WebSocket providers and listeners.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the anonymous POST handler receives request bodies from arbitrary clients.
walletAddress is taken directly from the request body and inserted into a process-global Set for every request, with no bound, expiration, or rate-limiting control.

The Set insertion is the memory-consumption sink; independently, the asynchronous check and initialization sequence can permit concurrent requests to create duplicate external WebSocket listeners before the flag is set.

title: Hardcoded MFA secrets and account credentials in test source
description: The test source embeds live-looking MFA seeds and account credentials as plaintext. For example, the existing wurstbrot account's TOTP seed is hardcoded at line 42 and is immediately used to generate a valid one-time password, while the corresponding account password is hardcoded at lines 140-142. Anyone who obtains the repository or test source can reproduce valid TOTP codes for that account and use the disclosed credentials against an environment where the fixture account exists. The additional setup and disable tests repeat this pattern with static passwords and TOTP secrets. Even if these are intended as test fixtures, they are authentication secrets stored in source and should be isolated, generated per test, or supplied through protected test configuration.

trace.description: The test entrypoint is the 2FA verification test, which constructs a request to the application endpoint; the caller is the test runner outside this file.
The test embeds the TOTP secret literal for the wurstbrot account and passes it to the OTP generator to create an authentication code.
The generated code and a signed temporary token for user ID 10 are sent to the 2FA verification endpoint, exercising authentication using the hardcoded secret.

A separate test embeds a static account password and TOTP setup secret, then sends the password and signed setup token to the 2FA setup endpoint, demonstrating repeated plaintext authentication material in source.

title: Hardcoded plaintext test account credential
description: The test setup contains the plaintext credential `ncc-1701` in source code and uses it to authenticate as `jim@juice-sh.op`. Anyone with access to the repository or test artifact can recover the credential and attempt authentication against an environment where this account exists. Although this is test code, the credential is hardcoded rather than supplied through a protected test-secret mechanism, and it may be reused accidentally in deployed or shared environments.
