The plaintext password `ncc-1701` is hardcoded in the repository and is passed into the authentication operation.

title: Continue-code workflow accepts codes for non-existent challenges
description: The test codifies successful acceptance of a continue code associated with a non-existent challenge: it sends an unauthenticated PUT request to the continue-code application endpoint and asserts HTTP 200. If this behavior reflects the production handler, an attacker can submit a fabricated or otherwise invalid code and advance workflow state without the server confirming that the referenced challenge exists. The route implementation is outside this file, so the finding is based on the explicitly expected behavior exercised here.

trace.description: Entrypoint: this test invokes the attacker-facing PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/:code endpoint; the route handler and its caller are outside this file.
The continue code is supplied in the URL path at line 105, with no prerequisite challenge lookup, existence proof, or authentication step represented in this test.
The test asserts HTTP 200 for a code explicitly described as belonging to non-existent challenge #999, establishing that the application is expected to accept this invalid workflow state.

title: Broken object-level authorization on baskets
description: The basket API permits authenticated object-level access without verifying that the authenticated user owns the requested basket. The test logs in as Bjoern, requests basket 2, and receives HTTP 200 with basket data. The same file also shows the authenticated Jim session applying a coupon to basket 2 and checking it out, indicating that basket identifiers can be substituted for another user's basket during sensitive operations. An attacker who knows or guesses another basket ID can read its contents and potentially perform checkout-related actions.

trace.description: The test invokes GET /rest/basket/:id with an authenticated token obtained for a distinct user; the route handler is outside this file.
The attacker-controlled basket identifier is supplied as /rest/basket/2, while the Authorization header contains the Bjoern user's token.
The response is accepted as 200 and contains basket id 2, with no ownership failure, proving that the requested object is returned to the authenticated caller.

title: Forged coupon accepted for a 99% discount
description: A coupon value explicitly named forgedCoupon is sent to the coupon endpoint for basket 2. The application accepts it and reports a 99% discount, after which checkout succeeds. This demonstrates that coupon authenticity/integrity can be bypassed and that the business workflow allows a forged discount to reduce the order price dramatically.

The forged coupon is supplied by the caller to PUT /rest/basket/2/coupon/:coupon.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200, indicating that the forged coupon passed validation.
The response confirms a 99% discount, and the subsequent checkout also succeeds, converting the validation failure into a material pricing/workflow impact.

title: Hardcoded account credentials in source
description: Multiple real account passwords are embedded directly in the test source, including the Jim account, Bjoern's account, and an administrator account. Anyone with access to the repository can obtain these credentials and attempt authentication against the corresponding environment; if the fixtures map to deployed or shared accounts, this enables account takeover or administrative access.

description: This test file embeds two plaintext passwords in calls to the authentication helper: the password for bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com at line 261 and the password for jim@juice-sh.op at line 330. Anyone who can read the repository can reuse those credentials against any reachable environment where these seeded accounts exist. The impact may be limited to test/demo accounts, but the credentials are nevertheless disclosed in source and could become dangerous if account data or deployment configuration is reused outside isolated tests.

title: Authenticated user can assign an orphaned basket item to an arbitrary basket
description: An authenticated caller can create a basket item without a BasketId and then set BasketId to an arbitrary value. The test expects PUT /api/BasketItems/:id with { BasketId: 3 } to return 200 and the response to contain BasketId 3. There is no evidence in this file of an ownership check ensuring that the selected basket belongs to the authenticated user. An attacker could use this relationship update to attach an item to another user's basket or otherwise manipulate basket ownership/state.

The request targets the newly created basket item's identifier and sends the caller-controlled relationship field BasketId with value 3 while authenticated with authHeader.
The test asserts a successful response and that the server accepted and returned BasketId 3, demonstrating persistence of the caller-selected basket relationship without a visible ownership check.

title: Hardcoded plaintext test account credentials
description: The test suite embeds the reusable plaintext credentials jim@juice-sh.op / ncc-1701 in source and uses them to obtain a bearer token. If this account exists in any non-isolated or deployed environment, anyone with repository or artifact access can authenticate as it. Even in a test-only deployment, retaining reusable credentials in source creates a credential-disclosure risk and should be replaced with injected, environment-specific test secrets.

The login helper is called with a fixed account email and plaintext password embedded in the source file.
The hardcoded password is explicitly present in the login input and is then exchanged for a bearer token used by subsequent authenticated requests.

title: Hardcoded Ethereum private key committed in test source
description: A plaintext Ethereum private key is embedded directly in the test source and submitted to the Web3 key endpoint. Anyone who can read the repository can recover this credential and use it to authenticate or solve the associated wallet challenge; if the key controls assets outside the test environment, those assets could also be compromised. Secrets should not be committed to source, including test files, unless they are provably non-sensitive and isolated test credentials.

The request body carries the hardcoded private key under the privateKey field and sends it to the application endpoint.
The plaintext private-key literal is present in repository source and is transmitted as a credential, exposing it to repository readers and any systems that retain or inspect the test code.

title: Plaintext administrative and user credentials committed in test source
description: The test source contains reusable account credentials, including the hardcoded administrative password `admin123`, and several other plaintext user passwords. If these fixtures correspond to accounts in a shared, deployed, or otherwise reachable environment, anyone with repository access can authenticate as those users, including the administrator. Even if intended only for tests, the credentials should be isolated to disposable test configuration and supplied through protected environment or fixture mechanisms rather than committed source.

title: Hardcoded plaintext account credentials in API tests
description: Plaintext credentials for test accounts are embedded directly in the source at lines 28, 54, 82, and 115. In particular, the ciso account password is supplied to the login helper and is associated with the configured application domain. Anyone who can read the repository can recover these credentials and attempt authentication against the corresponding environment; if the accounts or domain are shared with a reachable non-test deployment, this can provide unauthorized account access.

title: Plaintext application credentials hardcoded in test source
description: The test source embeds plaintext credentials for real-looking application accounts, including the Bjoern account password. Anyone with repository access can use these credentials against any environment where the account and password are still valid; the same pattern also appears for the admin account at line 321. Storing reusable authentication secrets in source is an insecure configuration and can lead to account compromise or administrative access.

The hardcoded credential is propagated into the login request through the helper call and is used to obtain a bearer token for subsequent API requests.

The resulting authenticated session is used to access the sensitive data-export endpoint, demonstrating that the literal is a reusable application credential rather than merely an inert fixture value.

title: CAPTCHA solution disclosed in API response, enabling challenge bypass
description: The CAPTCHA response is read from captchaRes.body.answer and that value is submitted as the CAPTCHA answer. This exposes the server-side solution to the client, allowing an attacker to request a CAPTCHA, read its answer from the JSON response, and immediately satisfy the supposedly protective challenge. The data-export operation therefore does not obtain meaningful protection from CAPTCHA enforcement.

The response is asserted successful and its body is subsequently treated as containing the CAPTCHA answer, showing that the solution is available to the client rather than retained only server-side.
The client submits captchaRes.body.answer directly to the data-export endpoint, providing a complete bypass path for the CAPTCHA challenge.

title: Hardcoded account credentials in source-controlled test code
description: The test source contains hardcoded usernames and passwords used by the login helper. The plaintext password at line 22 is directly committed in the repository, and equivalent credential literals are repeated throughout the file. If these accounts exist outside an isolated disposable test database, anyone with repository access can authenticate as them; if the credentials are reused in another environment, the exposure can extend beyond testing. Even for test-only accounts, embedding reusable credentials makes accidental promotion or environment reuse possible.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of encryption-key directory and premium AES key
description: The test demonstrates that an unauthenticated caller can enumerate the /encryptionkeys directory and retrieve the Premium Content AES key. Exposing encryption key material through a public static-file endpoint allows attackers to decrypt content intended to be protected and reveals internal security-sensitive files.

title: Public exposure of access log files
description: The test demonstrates that an unauthenticated caller can retrieve an access log file through a predictable application URL. Access logs may contain request paths, identifiers, IP addresses, tokens, or other operational data; serving them publicly enables information disclosure and undermines incident investigation.

The test expects HTTP 200 and an octet-stream response, confirming that the access log file is served successfully to the unauthenticated caller.
The response content type assertion further confirms that the endpoint returns a file rather than merely exposing a route that rejects access.

title: Hidden URL used as the only protection for premium content
description: The premium-content workflow relies on knowledge of an obscure URL rather than server-side authorization or payment verification. This file sends an unauthenticated request to the purported paywall URL and expects the premium image to be returned with HTTP 200, so any caller who discovers or guesses the path can bypass the intended payment prerequisite.

title: Feedback creation permits caller-controlled user impersonation
description: The feedback creation request accepts the UserId supplied by an unauthenticated caller. The test sends UserId 3 without an Authorization header and asserts a successful creation whose returned record has UserId 3. An attacker can therefore create feedback attributed to another account, enabling identity spoofing and corruption of user-owned feedback data. The authenticated test repeats the same issue with an arbitrary UserId.

The password is represented as a Base64 string, which is encoding rather than protection. Anyone with repository/source access can recover and attempt the credential against the test account or any environment where the same credential is reused. title: Public FTP route exposes confidential files and a KeePass database

A caller can request `/ftp/acquisitions.md` and receive HTTP 200 with confidential acquisition information; the adjacent KeePass test likewise expects `/ftp/incident-support.kdbx` to return HTTP 200. An attacker able to reach the endpoint can retrieve access-log contents, which may disclose request paths, identifiers, operational details, or other sensitive data and can aid incident reconnaissance. The separate traversal test only rejects forward slashes and does not mitigate exposure of valid log files.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of internal Prometheus metrics
description: The test demonstrates that an unauthenticated caller can request GET /metrics and receive HTTP 200. The endpoint exposes internal operational telemetry, including version information and registered-user counts asserted later in the same test file. If this route is deployed with the same access behavior, an external attacker can enumerate application metadata and usage statistics without authentication. The route implementation and any deployment-layer protection are outside this file, so production reachability is inferred from the test application's behavior.

title: Password change succeeds without verifying the current password

The test expects HTTP 200, confirming that the password-change workflow accepts an authenticated session as sufficient proof and does not require knowledge of the existing password. An attacker who obtains or hijacks a user's valid session can therefore change that user's password without the additional re-authentication control, potentially taking over the account.

title: Hardcoded account credentials and password-reset answers in test source

title: Predictable coupon encoding permits discount forgery
description: Coupon codes are demonstrated to be a reversible base85 encoding of the month, year, and discount rather than an unpredictable authenticated token. The acceptance test shows that a freshly generated code for an arbitrary discount, including 99, is accepted. An attacker can reproduce the encoding for the current period and submit a forged high-discount coupon if the surrounding purchase flow treats these codes as trusted bearer discounts.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies a discount and date to generateCoupon, and the test invokes it with an arbitrary discount value.
The test verifies that the resulting coupon decodes directly to the plaintext value JAN80-20, showing that the code is deterministic encoding rather than a secret or authenticated token.
The test confirms that a generated coupon with a high arbitrary discount of 99 is accepted by discountFromCoupon, demonstrating the business-logic sink for a forged current-period code.

title: Unlimited withdrawals allow a single caller to drain the faucet
description: The externally callable withdraw function transfers tokens to msg.sender without enforcing a per-address quota, cooldown, claim eligibility check, or other anti-drain control. A caller can invoke withdraw repeatedly, using successive amounts up to the remaining uint8 balance, until the faucet's balance reaches zero; subsequent calls revert because the subtraction is checked under Solidity 0.8. This allows one actor to monopolize funds intended for faucet users.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and enters the publicly callable withdraw(uint8 amount) function; no caller identity, claim history, or rate-limit state is checked.
The requested amount is subtracted from the shared faucet balance, with no per-caller accounting or restriction. The uint8 type limits one request but not repeated requests.
The requested amount is transferred to the caller, so repeated successful calls direct the shared token reserve to one address.

title: Withdrawals lack dedicated security audit events
description: The contract performs a security-relevant financial withdrawal but emits no event describing the caller, amount, or resulting balance. Although transactions are visible on-chain, the contract provides no dedicated withdrawal audit event for reliable monitoring and alerting, impairing detection and investigation of rapid faucet drainage.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and invokes the public withdrawal entrypoint.
The shared balance is changed as part of the withdrawal, but no event is emitted when this security-relevant state transition occurs.
Tokens are transferred to msg.sender without an accompanying emit statement recording the withdrawal details.

title: Unchecked ERC20 transfer result allows unpaid NFT mints
description: mintNFT attempts to collect mintPrice through IERC20.transferFrom but ignores the function's boolean return value. IERC20-compatible tokens may signal transfer failure by returning false rather than reverting. With such a token at the configured address, a caller can invoke mintNFT without successfully paying, while _safeMint still assigns the NFT. This violates the contract's apparent payment-for-mint invariant and can cause unpaid NFT issuance. The issue is certain in the contract logic; exploitability depends on the configured token implementing the permitted false-return behavior.

trace.description: mintNFT is externally callable by any caller; the caller is outside this file and becomes msg.sender, the address intended to pay and receive the NFT.
The contract requests mintPrice tokens from msg.sender using the externally configured IERC20 token, but does not verify the boolean result returned by transferFrom.
Regardless of whether transferFrom returned false, execution proceeds to _safeMint and creates the NFT for msg.sender, then records the mint as successful.

title: Reentrant withdrawal before balance accounting
description: withdraw performs the value transfer to msg.sender before decrementing balances[msg.sender]. During the callback, the recipient can reenter withdraw: the first call sets userWithdrawing to 1, and the nested call is still allowed because the guard accepts values less than or equal to 1. Both calls can pass the balance check against the unchanged balance and each transfer funds. The balance is decremented only after the calls return, and line 33 uses unchecked subtraction in Solidity 0.6 rather than SafeMath. Repeated exploitation can drain more ETH than the account's recorded balance and can cause an underflowed balance, enabling continued withdrawals up to the per-call limit.

trace.description: External callers enter the withdrawal workflow through withdraw; the caller and recipient contract are outside this file and control the callback behavior of msg.sender.
The contract checks the current balance and uses a counter that permits the first nested invocation: the outer call sets userWithdrawing to 1, while a reentrant call sees 1 and increments it to 2.
The contract invokes an arbitrary recipient-controlled fallback through msg.sender.call while the balance has not yet been reduced.

Only after the external call returns does the contract subtract the amount, so multiple successful nested calls can each transfer against the same pre-withdrawal balance; the raw subtraction can also underflow in Solidity 0.6.

title: Missing audit events for deposits and withdrawals
description: Ordinary financial security events are not emitted. ethdeposit updates a user's recorded balance without an event, and withdraw transfers ETH and changes the balance without an ordinary deposit or withdrawal event. The sole ContractExploited event is emitted only on the unusual guard path and is not a substitute for complete transaction monitoring. Operators relying on contract event logs cannot reliably reconstruct normal fund movements or detect anomalous withdrawal volume from the contract's own logs.

trace.description: An external caller enters the public withdrawal operation; the caller is outside this file.

The function validates the amount and balance and then performs a security-relevant ETH transfer and accounting mutation. No ordinary withdrawal event is emitted along this path; ContractExploited is emitted only for a special reentrancy-counter branch.

The balance is changed after the transfer without emitting an event identifying the user, amount, or resulting accounting state, leaving routine withdrawals absent from contract-level monitoring logs.

title: Deterministic textbook RSA permits public-key brute-force decryption
description: The script demonstrates a textbook RSA implementation whose ciphertexts can be decrypted without the private key because the plaintext domain is a small known character set. For each possible character, line 11 computes pow(ord(char), e, N) using the public exponent and modulus, and line 12 stores the resulting ciphertext-to-character mapping. Any ciphertext in announcement_encrypted.md can then be directly reversed at line 15. An attacker who obtains ciphertexts produced with the same scheme can reproduce this dictionary and recover the plaintext character by character, defeating confidentiality.

trace.description: The script receives ciphertext data from the local announcement_encrypted.md file; the caller or mechanism supplying this file is outside the target file.

For each character in a fixed, known alphabet, the code computes RSA encryption using the public exponent and modulus and records the ciphertext mapping. This creates a complete lookup table for the low-entropy plaintext domain.
The ciphertext strings are used as keys into the precomputed public dictionary, and the corresponding plaintext characters are emitted, recovering the message without private-key decryption.

title: Deterministic per-character textbook RSA leaks the document plaintext
description: The script uses textbook RSA without randomized padding and encrypts each character independently. For every ciphertext value, an observer who knows the public parameters can compute pow(ord(candidate), e, N) for likely characters and match the result. Repeated characters also produce repeated ciphertexts, exposing plaintext equality and formatting. Consequently, the confidential document can be reconstructed character-by-character from announcement_encrypted.md without factoring N or obtaining the private key.

trace.description: Top-level script entrypoint: the confidential input is read from announcement.md; content supplied or modified by the caller/environment enters this file here.
The script defines a public RSA modulus and exponent (N and e), which are sufficient for an attacker to compute candidate ciphertexts for likely plaintext characters.
The plaintext is consumed one character at a time, preserving a direct per-character relationship between input characters and output ciphertexts.

Each character is encrypted with raw pow(ord(char), e, N) and written as a separate ciphertext line. There is no OAEP/randomized padding or other concealment, so public-key dictionary matching and frequency analysis recover plaintext characters.

title: Hardcoded RSA private key and unauthenticated textbook RSA decryption
description: The RSA private parameters N and d are hardcoded in the source at lines 5-6. Anyone who obtains this file obtains the private key and can decrypt ciphertexts produced for the corresponding RSA public key. The script also performs raw textbook RSA decryption at line 9, without OAEP padding or any integrity/authentication mechanism, so ciphertext is accepted and decrypted without authenticity verification. This can expose plaintext and permits attackers to submit crafted ciphertexts if the script is used as a decryption service or oracle.

trace.description: Module execution begins outside this file; at module load, the script defines the RSA modulus and private exponent as source-code constants.

The hardcoded private parameters remain available to the decryption operation, while ciphertext is read from the fixed local file. No key loading, secret protection, authenticity check, or padding configuration is present.

Each input line is converted to an integer and decrypted with raw modular exponentiation using the exposed private exponent; the resulting plaintext is printed without authentication or integrity verification.

title: Unbounded ciphertext input and repeated expensive RSA operations
description: The script calls readlines() without any input-size limit, retaining the complete file in memory. It then performs a computationally expensive modular exponentiation with a very large private exponent for every line. If an attacker can supply or replace announcement_encrypted.md in the execution environment, a sufficiently large file or many lines can cause excessive memory and CPU consumption. The attacker-controlled file condition is not established within this source file.

trace.description: The script is invoked by a caller outside this file and opens the fixed input file; whether an attacker can control that file is not shown here.
All input lines are loaded at once with readlines(), with no file-size, line-count, or ciphertext-length limit.
A large modular exponentiation is performed separately for every line, and the accumulated plaintext is joined and printed, allowing oversized input to consume substantial memory and CPU.

title: Unpinned Alpine base image permits mutable or compromised build contents
description: The Dockerfile builds from the mutable `alpine` tag rather than a pinned Alpine version or image digest. Each build can therefore consume different base-image contents, including newly introduced vulnerable packages or an image changed through registry or supply-chain compromise. Because this is a smoke-test image, the direct production impact may be limited, but the configuration undermines build integrity and reproducibility and could allow malicious code to run during the test container's execution.

trace.description: The Docker build receives the external `alpine` image reference as its base image; the image source and tag resolution are controlled outside this file.
The build installs `curl` into whatever contents are supplied by the mutable base image, inheriting its changing package ecosystem and trust assumptions.
The resulting image executes the smoke test from that unpinned base at the configured application URL, so altered or vulnerable base contents are present at runtime.

title: Unredacted smoke-test URL may expose credentials in CI logs
description: The script logs the complete value of its externally supplied target URL with printf. URLs can contain sensitive material such as HTTP basic-auth credentials or access tokens in query parameters. When the smoke test runs in CI, this value may be captured in build logs and exposed to users with log access. The script does not redact credentials or sensitive query components before printing the URL.

trace.description: The script receives the launch target from its first positional argument; the caller and any source of that value are outside this file.
The supplied target is propagated directly as the printf substitution value, with no parsing or redaction of userinfo, query parameters, or tokens.
printf writes the complete target URL to standard output, which is commonly retained as CI/build log data.

title: Juice Shop container exposed on all host interfaces
description: The Juice Shop container is published using `-p 3000:3000`, which by default binds the host port on all interfaces. A network attacker who can reach the VM can connect directly to port 3000 and bypass Apache and any access controls, headers, routing restrictions, or TLS policy configured in the Apache front end. This exposes the application’s administrative and intentionally vulnerable routes directly at the container port.

trace.description: The Vagrant provisioning process invokes this shell script; the caller and reachable network context are outside this file.
The script downloads and starts the Juice Shop Docker image as the deployed application service.

Docker publishes container port 3000 as host port 3000 without `127.0.0.1:` or another restricted bind address, exposing the service on all host interfaces and allowing direct access that bypasses Apache.

title: MD5 used for package integrity checksums
description: The checksum task generates MD5 digests for every file in dist/ and writes them as verification artifacts. MD5 is collision-prone and unsuitable as a security integrity mechanism: an attacker able to replace a packaged artifact can potentially create a different artifact with the same MD5, undermining consumers that treat these files as authenticity or tamper evidence. No stronger hash or signature is generated here.

trace.description: The exported Grunt configuration is invoked by a caller outside this file; the caller can run the registered packaging task.
The package task invokes checksum after creating the distribution archive, making the generated digest the package verification artifact.
The task creates an MD5 hash with crypto.createHash('md5') and writes the resulting digest to a .md5 file.

title: Unvalidated build parameters control archive output path
description: The archive filename is assembled from Grunt options and environment variables without restricting them to safe filename components. A caller that can control the build invocation or CI environment can supply values such as '../outside' and cause the compression task to target a path outside the intended dist/ directory, depending on the archive plugin's path handling. This can overwrite or create artifacts in unintended locations and compromise build output integrity.

trace.description: The exported Grunt function receives options and environment state from a caller outside this file.
The os, platform, and node values are read directly from Grunt options or environment variables without a safe filename-component allow-list.
Those values are interpolated into the archive path under dist/; traversal components can alter the output location if accepted by the compression task.

title: Distribution archive includes cryptographic key material
description: The distributable archive explicitly contains ctf.key and the encryptionkeys directory. If these files contain private signing, encryption, or application key material—as their names indicate—every recipient of the generated package receives the key material, allowing decryption, forgery, or compromise of data protected by those keys. The file provides no exclusion, environment-specific handling, or secret-management control.

trace.description: The exported build configuration is executed by an external caller to produce a distribution archive.
The compression task's source list includes the ctf.key file and all files beneath encryptionkeys without filtering or conditional exclusion.
The compression task packages those paths into the distributable archive.

title: Unauthenticated LLM tool can generate unauthorized coupons
description: POST /rest/chat is registered without authentication, and the handler exposes generateCoupon to the LLM. The coupon policy exists only as natural-language instructions in the system prompt; generateCoupon itself accepts any numeric discount and calls security.generateCoupon without checking authentication, a verified damaged order, a valid order ID, return rejection, or the 10% maximum. An attacker can send a chat request directing the chatbot to generate a coupon, or attempt to induce a tool call with a discount above 10%, and the server-side tool will create it if the model invokes the tool. This crosses an authorization boundary because eligibility is decided by model behavior rather than an independent server check.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported chat handler receives requests for POST /rest/chat; the route registration and caller are outside this file, and the supplied route context declares no authentication middleware.

The handler accepts caller-controlled messages from req.body and constructs an LLM invocation with the generateCoupon tool available. The coupon requirements at lines 97-104 are prompt text only, not an authorization check.

The model-controlled tool input is only validated as an arbitrary number; execute immediately generates a coupon without checking user identity, order eligibility, return rejection, or the maximum discount.

title: Public chat accepts unbounded LLM workloads
description: The public chat endpoint forwards the entire caller-supplied messages value to the LLM without an application-level limit on request body size, number of messages, message length, or total token budget. The handler also has no visible rate limiting. Repeated requests containing very large message histories can cause excessive request parsing, token processing, LLM API consumption, and streaming work. External proxy or body-parser limits may reduce impact, but no such control is present in this file.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported chat handler receives unauthenticated POST /rest/chat requests; route registration is outside this file and declares no authentication middleware.
The request body messages value is accepted with only a fallback and no visible schema, size, count, or token limit.

The unbounded messages value is passed directly into streamText, causing the configured LLM provider to process the attacker-selected workload; no per-request rate or workload cap is enforced in this handler.

title: Authenticated users can request arbitrary basket IDs
description: The basket endpoint accepts a caller-selected basket identifier and applies only the generic authenticated-user middleware before invoking retrieveBasket. No middleware in this file binds the identifier to the authenticated user's ID, unlike the separate /rest/basket middleware pattern that uses security.appendUserId(). If retrieveBasket does not independently enforce ownership, User A can request User B's basket ID and obtain its contents.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches GET /rest/basket/:id, where :id is supplied by the requester and is passed to retrieveBasket().
The route is covered only by security.isAuthorized() at the /rest/basket/:id mount; this verifies authentication but does not visibly append or compare the basket owner.
The caller-controlled basket ID is handed to the imported retrieveBasket handler, with no ownership check visible between the route registration and handler invocation.

title: Generated CRUD APIs permit unrestricted model-property binding
description: finale automatically creates CRUD endpoints for multiple models. Most resources use exclude: [], and finale receives no explicit property allow-list. This means request bodies can be automatically bound to any persisted model attributes exposed by the ORM, including fields that may represent ownership, roles, status, pricing, or other server-controlled state. The empty exclusion configuration is especially fragile because future sensitive model fields become writable by default.

trace.description: An external caller can reach the generated /api/{Model}s and /api/{Model}s/:id CRUD endpoints registered by this file.

Each model is registered with finale using excludeAttributes from the model configuration; Product, Feedback, BasketItem, Complaint, Recycle, Address, Card, Quantity, Hint, and other resources use empty exclusion arrays.
finale.resource automatically wires model create/update operations, with no explicit caller-field allow-list shown before persistence.

title: Global permissive CORS configuration
description: The application-wide CORS middleware is configured with cors() defaults and the comment explicitly states that everything is allowed. It is installed for all origins and all routes, including authenticated APIs. This permits arbitrary websites to make cross-origin requests to the application; if any authentication mechanism or deployment configuration permits credentialed requests, sensitive API responses can be exposed cross-origin. Even without cookies, the setting unnecessarily broadens the attack surface for bearer-authenticated APIs.

trace.description: An attacker-controlled website can issue browser cross-origin requests to the Express application handled by this file.
CORS is enabled globally with cors() and no origin allow-list, credential policy, or route restriction; OPTIONS requests are also globally enabled.
The global middleware emits permissive CORS behavior for subsequent authenticated and sensitive endpoints.

title: Hardcoded weak cookie-signing secret
description: cookie-parser is initialized with the source-code literal 'kekse' as its signing secret. Any signed cookie used by the application can be forged by an attacker who knows this publicly visible value, potentially changing trusted cookie state or bypassing controls that rely on signed-cookie integrity.

trace.description: Every incoming HTTP request reaches the application cookie parsing middleware.
The middleware is configured with the hardcoded secret literal 'kekse' rather than a deployment secret.
cookieParser uses that predictable, source-visible value to verify signed cookies, allowing attackers to generate valid signatures for modified cookie values.

title: Internal directories and log files are publicly mounted
description: The application exposes directory indexes and file-serving handlers for /ftp, /.well-known, /encryptionkeys, and /support/logs. In particular, /support/logs mounts serve-index before the challenge middleware and then serves arbitrary named log files. These routes can disclose operational files, logs, keys, or other internal resources if the backing directories contain them and the challenge middleware is not an actual authorization barrier.

trace.description: An external requester can access the directory and file routes mounted under /ftp, /encryptionkeys, and /support/logs.
Directory listing is enabled with serveIndex and file handlers are mounted directly; /support/logs lists the directory before the challenge middleware is installed.
servePublicFiles, serveKeyFiles, and serveLogFiles serve files selected by request paths, exposing internal resources when present in those directories.

title: Generated list endpoints have unbounded result sets
description: All finale-generated CRUD resources explicitly disable pagination. Public or broadly accessible list endpoints can therefore load the complete table into memory and serialize it in one response. An attacker can repeatedly request large collections as the database grows, consuming database, application memory, CPU, and bandwidth.

trace.description: A caller can request collection endpoints such as the generated /api/Products, /api/Feedbacks, /api/Recycles, and other model lists.
The generated resource configuration applies to every model in autoModels, including resources with empty exclusions and broad read access.
